paragraphs.text: De rebus retentionum - that is, concerning the drought or dearth by restraint of necessary rain and moisture - unde frugum raritas, annonae caritas, fames, from which the shortage of grain made the year’s produce expensive, resulting in famine; whereupon followed a famine, as there doth also a "famine of the Word," where the divine influences are restrained. Junius rendereth it, Super verbis cohibitionum, concerning the words of cohibitions; that is, saith he, concerning the prayers made by the prophet and other good people for the diverting of God’s judgments, publicly denounced.
paragraphs.anchor: The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah concerning the dearth.

paragraphs.text: The prophet’s pitiful complaint, bitterly bewailing the common calamity, and labouring thereby to bring them to a sense of the true cause of it, their sins. See 2Sa 21:1. {See Trapp on "2Sa 21:1"}
paragraphs.anchor: Judah mourneth.

paragraphs.text: sc., To heaven, for removal of this judgment. Compare Jer 36:9; Jer 14:12.
paragraphs.anchor: And the cry of Jerusalem is gone up

paragraphs.text: Who would be sure to have it if it were to be had.
paragraphs.anchor: And their nobles.

paragraphs.text: Their boys, as they used to call their menial servants of the younger sort. See Mat 14:2. {See Trapp on "Mat 14:2"}
paragraphs.anchor: Sent their little ones.

paragraphs.text: Such as were the waters of Siloe, which only fountain, saith Jerome, Jerusalem maketh use of so long as it lasteth.
paragraphs.anchor: To the waters.

paragraphs.text: Or, Cisterns. {Jer 2:13}
paragraphs.anchor: To the pits

paragraphs.text: As close mourners do still.
paragraphs.anchor: They covered their heads.

paragraphs.text: As our hearts also are and will be, when the heaven doth not hear the earth. {as Hos 2:21} It hath been before observed, that in the use of the ordinances, if we open our shells (our souls), the heaven will drop the fruitful dew of grace to the making of pearls of good works and solid virtue.
paragraphs.anchor: Because the ground is chapt.

paragraphs.text: The loving hind; {Pro 5:19} Alioqui studiosa sui partus, {a} that is otherwise so exceeding chary and careful of her young.
paragraphs.anchor: Yea, the hind also calved in the field, and forsook it.

paragraphs.text: {a} Plin., lib. viii. cap. 32.
Secretes alias vagae libidinis in silvis, that usually course up and down the woods, and can bear hunger and thirst a long while together. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: And the wild asses.

paragraphs.text: Quorum est vehementissima spiratio ac sorbitio; who, in defect of water, can continue long by drawing in the air, as Aristotle {b} likewise testifieth of the goats in Cephalonia, that they drink not for various days together, but instead thereof gape and suck in the fresh air.
paragraphs.anchor: Snuffed up the wind like dragons.

paragraphs.text: {a} Plin., lib. x. cap. 72.
{b} Lib. De mirab auscult.
Though our guilty consciences bring in large rolls of indictment written against us within and without, and spread before thee.
paragraphs.anchor: O Lord, though our iniquities testify against us.

paragraphs.text: Do it for thy name’s sake.] Heb., Do. A short but pithy petition. So Jer 14:9, "Leave us not."
In prayer, to pitch upon such of God’s attributes as wherein we may see an answer, is a high point of heavenly wisdom.
paragraphs.anchor: O the Hope of Israel, the Saviour thereof.

paragraphs.text: As a stranger at home, and as one that is loath to be too busy in aliena republica, in a foreign land where he hath least to do.
paragraphs.anchor: Why shouldest thou be as a stranger in the land?

paragraphs.text: Into some diversorium - inn.
paragraphs.anchor: That turneth aside.

paragraphs.text: That knows not which way to take: first he goes one way, and by and by he returns again. Tremellius rendereth it ut vir fatiscens, as one that fainteth, hath done his utmost, and can do no more.
paragraphs.anchor: Why shouldest thou be as a man astonished?

paragraphs.text: Extingui lucem nec patiare tuam. This was to "stir up himself to take hold of God."
paragraphs.anchor: Yet thou, O Lord, art in the midst of us; leave us not.

paragraphs.text: Therefore now they shall have enough of it; yet not wander so wide as to miss hell; {Psa 95:10-11} what wonder that God seemed a stranger to them who had so far estranged themselves from him?
paragraphs.anchor: They have loved to wander.

paragraphs.text: See on Jer 7:16.
paragraphs.anchor: Pray not for this people.

paragraphs.text: At their fasts they were wont to pray earnestly, and to make their voices to be heard on high. Sed defuit aliquid intas; their hearts cried not.
paragraphs.anchor: When they fast I will not hear their cry.

paragraphs.text: The Vulgate Latin hath it, Ah, ah, ah. Vide diligentissimam intercessionem. He seeketh somewhat to excuse the people by laying the blame upon their false prophets. Like whereunto were those Popish priests in Gerson’s time, who preached publicly to the people, that whosoever would come to hear a mass, he should not be struck blind on that day, neither should he die a sudden death, nor want sufficient sustenance, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: Ah, Lord God!

paragraphs.text: Heb., Peace of truth. Thus these deluders had learned to speak the language of God’s true prophets. Of the high soaring, pretended spiritual language of Familists and some other sectarians one saith well, That it is a great deal too high for this world, and a great deal too low for the world to come.
paragraphs.anchor: But I will give you assured peace.

paragraphs.text: These are certain signs of impostors in the Church in all ages, against whom, now, if ever, the temple doors had need be well guarded, and the pulpit doors have written on them, Oυδεις εισιτω αναξιος, Let no unworthy creature presume to come here.
paragraphs.anchor: The prophets prophesy falsely in my name, &c.

paragraphs.text: Heb., They are saying. This is all their song, though the present famine doth in part confute them; but the people were willing enough to be deceived, and were therefore worthily punished. Being infatuated, they were seduced; and being so seduced, they were justly judged, as Augustine somewhere. The blind led the blind, and both fell into the ditch, though it befell the blind guides to lie nethermost.
paragraphs.anchor: Yet they say.

paragraphs.text: They shall be no more excused by their having been deluded, than he that in his drink committeth adultery or murder is excused by his drunkenness. A drunkard, saith Aristotle, deserveth double punishment: {a} first for his drunkenness, and then for the sin committed in and by his drunkenness; so here. See on Jer 14:15.
paragraphs.anchor: And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out.

paragraphs.text: {a} τοις μεθυουσι διπλα τα επιτιμια. - Ethic., lib. iii. cap. 5.
This the prophet did doubtless in good earnest; like as Samuel mourned for the rejection of Saul, and our Saviour wept over Jerusalem.
paragraphs.anchor: Let mine eyes run down.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Be silent; for tears also have a voice, {Psa 39:12} and do oft prove very effectual orators.
paragraphs.anchor: And let them not cease.

paragraphs.text: The prophet here sets forth the siege as present, though it was many years after, the more to affect the people.
paragraphs.anchor: If I go forth into the field.

paragraphs.text: Or, Go about the land - sc., begging their bread, or fleeing their miseries - and men know them not, though men of such rank and quality.
paragraphs.anchor: Yea, both the prophet and the priest go about into a land that they know not.

paragraphs.text: So as that I may not put up one prayer more for them. I cannot hold, whatever come of it; let not my Lord be angry if I shoot this arrow also after the former.
paragraphs.anchor: Hast thou utterly rejected Judah?

paragraphs.text: We, the better sort of us, do so. And so the saints have ever done in their interdealings with God, falling low at his footstool for pardoning and prevailing mercy.
paragraphs.anchor: We acknowledge, O Lord, our wickedness.

paragraphs.text: Do not abhor us, for thy name’s sake.] This was to "continue instant in prayer." {Rom 12:12} This was to pray on, and not to faint. {Luk 18:1} If thy suit be not honest, never begin it; and if it be, never leave it.

The temple, and the ark in it. The Romans held the extinction of the Vestal fire a sign of the destruction of their city, be the cause thereof what it will. {a} We may well think the same of the loss of God’s ordinances, which therefore we must deprecate, as here, with all our might; for as Bodin said well of obtaining, so likewise for retaining, religion, Non disputationibus sed rogationibus, &c., the business will be the better ejected by requests than disputes. Pray therefore for the peace of Jerusalem, yea, take no nay. Deus ipse qui nullis contra se viribus superari potest, precibus vincitur. {b} The invincible God is overcome by the power of prayer. There is a kind of omnipotence in it, saith Luther.
paragraphs.anchor: Do not disgrace the throne of thy glory.

paragraphs.text: Lo, this is to be God’s faithful remembrancer, {Isa 62:6-7} suggesting unto him seasonable items.
paragraphs.anchor: Remember, break not thy covenant with us.

paragraphs.text: {a} εφ ης ποτε αν αιτιας γενηται. - Dion. Halicar., lib. ii.
{b} Jerome.
i.e., The heathen idols wickedly worshipped by the Jews.
paragraphs.anchor: Are there among the vanities of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: Pluit, ningit: supple Deus. These impersonals imply that the ancient Romans looked upon rain, snow, &c., as God’s work. Sure it is that they come by a divine decree. {Job 28:26} Not Jupiter, ομβριος - whatever the poets fable - nor the heavens themselves, without the divine concurrence, can give rain; but it is God Almighty who both prepareth it {Psa 147:8} and withholdeth it at his pleasure. {Amo 4:7} The second causes do but serve the divine providence in these common occurrences.
paragraphs.anchor: That can cause rain?

paragraphs.text: For seasonable showers in this our great necessity. We will wait, or, if thou see fit, want of our will, so that thy will may be done; for that is best.
paragraphs.anchor: Therefore we will wait upon thee.

paragraphs.text: Both the constellations, and rain or drought caused thereby.
paragraphs.anchor: For thou hast made all these things.
